name: Chachapoyas Quechua
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
sweep_summary: The only works with stress in the title, Valqui & Chalco 2023 (Pontes, vol. 2, pp. 241-273; doi 10.29327/5382304.1-7), is squarely about Chachapoyas Quechua stress but could not be read: the DOI lands on a Pontes product page where the ebook is free but delivered only through a WooCommerce cart/checkout; OpenAlex marks it closed with no repository copy, archive. an open Brid 2024 review on SciELO Uruguay was also unreachable). The stress statement is nevertheless settled first-hand by the same author's open doctoral thesis (Valqui 2020, p. 152, held by the project): primary stress on the first syllable of the word with rhythmic right-to-left secondary stresses, no noun/verb split — which confirms the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding and supersedes its current deciding source (Wikipedia paraphrasing Urban 2021, itself a second-hand line citing Taylor 1979). Valqui 2018 (Letras, p. 91) refines with a penult variant in some verbs and possible rhythmic secondary stress.

new_statements.translation: In Chachapoyas Quechua, accentual prominence is assigned to the first syllable of the word, with secondary stresses built rhythmically from right to left on every two stressable metrical elements.

new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary word stress for nouns and verbs alike (a single parameter setting: Left-Left-Left edge, iterative left-headed binary constituents, *(x( clash prevention), with rhythmic secondary stress. Based on the author's own acoustic field data from Chachapoyas and Luya provinces.

new_statements.quote: [p. 256, §3.2 'Unidades suprasegmentales: el acento'] A diferencia de otras variedades del quechua II que presentan acento en la penúltima sílaba, el quechua de Chachapoyas asigna su acento principal en el extremo izquierdo de la palabra prosódica. [...] [p. 268, §4 Conclusiones] Con respecto a los patrones acentuales, se ha registrado un acento regular en el extremo izquierdo de la palabra prosódica sin importar el número de sílabas ni la categoría gramatical. Un posible acento secundario se ha registrado en los verbos compuestos por más de 4 sílabas. Enunciados ubicados al final de cláusula y con énfasis muestran el acento principal en la antepenúltima o penúltima sílaba de la palabra.
new_statements.translation: [p. 256] Unlike other Quechua II varieties, which have stress on the penultimate syllable, Chachapoyas Quechua assigns its main stress at the left edge of the prosodic word. [...] [p. 268] As for the stress patterns, a regular stress has been recorded at the left edge of the prosodic word regardless of the number of syllables or the grammatical category. A possible secondary stress has been recorded in verbs of more than 4 syllables. Utterances at the end of a clause and under emphasis show the main stress on the antepenultimate or penultimate syllable of the word.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed-dominant initial, initial stress) and as both statements held by the project (Valqui 2020 thesis: initial primary stress; Weber 1975: 'casi únicamente en la primera sílaba'). Adds detail: initial stress holds for nouns and verbs regardless of length (2-5 syllables, acoustic evidence), a possible secondary stress on the penult of long verbs, and a phrase-level shift of primary stress to the penult/antepenult under emphasis and clause-finally. The secondary-stress description differs in form from the 2020 thesis statement held by the project (there: rhythmic right-to-left binary secondary stresses; here: a possible penult secondary stress in verbs o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls regularly on the first syllable (left edge of the prosodic word) in nouns and verbs alike, whatever the number of syllables (shown with pitch contours, vowel duration and formant centralization for 2- to 5-syllable words: [ˈkuŋgurniː], [ˈpirkakə̥na], [ˈrunakə̥nata]); unstressed later vowels shorten, centralize, and final high vowels devoice or drop. Verbs of four or more syllables show a possible secondary prominence (tonal rise) on the penult ([ˈtaktaɾkansa], [ˈkatʃpatʃiɾkansa]). Under emphasis and clause-finally the main stress moves to the penult (or antepenult) ([ˌmiku̥ˈʃani̥] 'he comido'). The authors attribute initial stress to Proto-Quechua inheritance rather than a Chacha substrate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'possible secondary stress' on the penultimate syllable of verbs of more than four syllables, seen as a rise in the tonal contour (pp. 261-263, 268); nouns of 4-5 syllables show only the initial high tone with a steady fall (pp. 259-261).
new_statements.exceptions: In emphatic utterances and at the end of a clause the primary stress shifts to the penultimate (or, clause-finally in one subordinate-clause example, the antepenultimate) syllable, in nouns and verbs alike (pp. 263-265, 268); the clause-final antepenult case is flagged as 'un contexto aún por estudiar con mayor detalle' (p. 264). Data: 6 speakers from Lamud, Colcamar (Luya prov.) and La Jalca, Granada, Olleros (Chachapoyas prov.), 150-word elicitation list plus narratives, Praat analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Chachapoyas Quechua (quechua de Chachapoyas / quechua amazonense, Quechua IIB), southern Amazonas department, Peru: data from Lamud and Colcamar (Luya province) and La Jalca, Granada and Olleros (Chachapoyas province); 6 speakers (2 men, 4 women); Lamud described as the most conservative variety, Granada-Olleros the most innovative (monophthongization), stress pattern the same in all five towns.

new_statements.quote: 1.3.8 La acentuación es casi únicamente en la primera sílaba. Con esto, al final de la palabra se desonorizan mucho las vocales, o se las pierde: šamušan /šamu+ša+ni/ 'He venido.' rípanAY wásinčItA 'Vamos a nuestra casa.' mana wásixUčU kani 'No tengo casa.' kami mákorkikI /kam maka+wa+rka+yki/ 'Tú me pegaste.' A veces hay una acentuación secundaria: če mákašUykItáka 'él que me pegó' paytA káwarkáni 'A él ví.' [...] A veces la entonación sube en la última sílaba: míkunene↑ áyčata 'Quiero comer carne.'
new_statements.translation: 1.3.8 Stress is almost exclusively on the first syllable. As a result, at the end of the word the vowels are heavily devoiced, or lost: [examples: 'I have come', 'Let's go to our house', 'I have no house', 'You hit me']. Sometimes there is a secondary stress: [examples: 'the one who hit me', 'I saw him'] ... Sometimes the intonation rises on the last syllable: [example: 'I want to eat meat'].

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial stress = initial) and as Valqui Culqui 2020 (primary prominence on the first syllable). Adds: the 'almost exclusively' hedge, optional secondary stress (examples show it on the penult, compatible with Valqui's right-to-left rhythmic secondary accents), word-final vowel devoicing/loss as a correlate of initial stress, and occasional utterance-final intonation rise. Independent 1974 field data (Weber, D. Coombs, H. Coombs; two-day visit to Lamud, Luya province), 45 years before Valqui's acoustic study.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls almost exclusively on the first syllable of the word; as a consequence word-final vowels are strongly devoiced or dropped. Occasionally a secondary stress appears later in the word (in every marked example it sits on the penult: mákašUykItáka, káwarkáni, ápamUšánču, tárpukUšúnčU), and occasionally sentence intonation rises on the final syllable (marked with an up-arrow; treated as intonation, not word stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'A veces hay una acentuación secundaria' — an optional secondary stress; the four transcribed examples all carry it on the penultimate syllable with primary stress on the initial syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'casi únicamente' (almost exclusively) initial, with no non-initial primary-stress examples given; final-syllable intonation rise in some utterances (questions/exclamations) is noted separately as intonation. Introduction (printed p. 4) notes one informant from San Cristóbal de Olto whose speech differed in segmental details (no note on stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Weber 1975 describes the Quechua of Lamud (Luya province, Amazonas, Peru), a Chachapoyas Quechua locality; data from a two-day visit in January 1974 with three informants native to Lamud and one from San Cristóbal de Olto (whose speech differed in some segmental details). Glottolog files the work under Chachapoyas Quechua [quk]; it is the same language as the catalog entry, not a different variety.

tone.quote: En el quechua de Amazonas, la prominencia acentual se asigna en la primera sílaba de la palabra, con acentos secundarios que se construyen de manera rítmica de derecha a izquierda por cada dos elementos métricos acentuables. Los correlatos acústicos del acento en esta variedad se evidencian en los valores formánticos, la duración vocálica y la frecuencia fundamental (F0). ... En términos del F0, como se puede observar en la Figura 3, la prominencia tonal representada por el tono alto (H*) se asocia con la primera sílaba de la palabra.
tone.locator: §3.3 'El acento en el quechua de Amazonas', pp. 59-60
tone.translation: In Amazonas Quechua, stress prominence is assigned to the first syllable of the word, with secondary stresses built rhythmically from right to left every two stressable metrical elements. The acoustic correlates of stress in this variety show up in formant values, vowel duration and fundamental frequency (F0). ... In terms of F0, as can be seen in Figure 3, the tonal prominence represented by the high tone (H*) is associated with the first syllable of the word.
tone.summary: No lexical tone described: pitch (H* high tone) is an exponent of predictable word-initial primary stress, alongside duration and vowel quality; secondary stresses rhythmic right-to-left; unstressed high vowels devoice/elide. Source does not use the words 'not tonal'.

sources.note: Morphophonological/acoustic study of short vs long monophthongized vowels in the 1st/2nd person possessor suffixes of Chachapoyas Quechua; it explicitly engages the earlier account in which STRESS ('el acento') was held responsible for the short/long alternations [i]/[i:], [e]/[e:] and proposes instead an underspecified [coronal] initial segment; touches stress as an explanatory factor, no tone content; not opened (UNMSM host behind Anubis).
